title: The Old Gods of the Holds
subtitle: Fate, Making and Memory
summary: The faith of the north: an unfinished world, the Great Weave, the final death of being forgotten, and the gods Expeditioners still name at the Gates.
content:
> *"Then let it burn where no roof can contain it."*
> — Veyr, in the Forging of the Sun

The dominant indigenous faith of the [Vardic Holds](factions.html#vardic-holds) is the worship of the **Old Gods**. It is less a single church than a shared way of understanding the world, built around three ideas: **Fate**, **Making** and **Memory**.

In the Vardic view the world is not a finished creation. Creation is still going on, and both gods and mortals take part in shaping what the world becomes. That is why craft carries religious weight in the Holds. Making something that did not exist before is one of the ways a person leaves a mark on existence, and a well-made ship, engine or blade is, in a small way, an act of faith.

The Old Gods remain culturally dominant across the north. A minority in the ports follows the [[faith-of-the-first-light|Faith of the First Light]] (see *The First Light in the Holds*, below).

## The Great Weave

The most common Vardic image of the world is the **Great Weave**. Everything leaves a thread in it: people, gods, places, objects, deeds, promises and creations.

Fate, in this picture, is not a script written in advance. It is closer to the tension of all those threads pulling on one another. Nobody can control every force acting on them. What a person *can* control is the kind of thread they leave behind.

This is why the Vards care so much about action, reputation and consequence. A promise is a thread. So is a betrayal. So is a ship, and the name painted on it.

The finer workings of the Weave are not agreed on. Some Holds tell it one way and some another, and the Vards are generally comfortable leaving it so.

## Memory and the Final Death

To the Vards, memory has metaphysical weight. A person can die in body without being entirely gone. They continue through their family, through stories, named objects, inscriptions, accomplishments, songs and obligations that others still remember.

The worst death is to be forgotten completely. It is often called the **final death**.

That belief explains much of Vardic culture: the sagas, the inscriptions, the named ships and the maker's marks, the preserved ancestral halls, the habit of reciting what the dead did. Foreigners often mistake all this for vanity. To many Vards it is closer to a small religious act: keeping a thread from going slack.

What lies beyond death, if anything, is described differently from Hold to Hold, and the old stories say surprisingly little about it. The tradition cares more *that* the dead are remembered than *where* they go.

> **At a funeral in a shipyard Hold**
>
> The reciter stood at the head of the hall with no notes. She did not need any.
>
> "Bjarni Holt. Rebuilt the north slip after the fire. Taught forty apprentices, and all forty can still rivet. Swore to see his sister's children grown, and saw it. Lost two fingers to the Ironmouth press and named the press anyway."
>
> She stopped, and the hall waited.
>
> One by one, the mourners stood and added a thing he had done that she had missed. A loan never asked back. A song he sang badly. The night he held the gate during the strike.
>
> When nobody else stood, the reciter said the old closing words: "Now he is ours to remember."

## The Gods

The Old Gods are many, and each Hold honours some more than others. Five figures are known everywhere in the north.

**Veyr, the First Smith**, is the god of fire, craftsmanship, invention, endurance and making. Veyr stands for the idea that creation demands skill, discipline and transformation, and sometimes the destruction of an old form. Smiths, engineers, machinists and craftspeople of every kind invoke Veyr.

**Ragna of the Far Shore** belongs to the sea, to voyages and exploration, to unknown horizons, and to those who leave and those who do not come back. Sailors and explorers have always honoured her. Since the Gates appeared, she has become the patron most Vardic Expeditioners name first.

**Haldor the Oathkeeper** watches over promises, law, hospitality and agreements, and brings vengeance on oathbreakers. Vards invoke Haldor at treaties, marriages, political agreements and any promise serious enough to matter.

**Skara Under the Mountain** is the goddess of death, ancestry, memory and buried things, and of the solemn bond between the living and the dead. Skara is not an evil death-goddess. Her role is grave rather than sinister, and funerals and acts of remembrance are often made in her name.

**The Wanderer Without a Name** is the least certain of them: a figure of strangers, luck, altered identity, unexpected discovery and events that change the world. The stories never quite agree on what the Wanderer wants, and that uncertainty is part of the Wanderer's nature.

> **In a Furnace District engine hall**
>
> The new boiler had passed every test. Before the foreman would let anyone fire it for real, the oldest smith on the floor walked once around it, laid a sooty palm on the maker's mark, and spoke quietly.
>
> "Veyr, it's made. It's as good as our hands could make it. Now let it become what it will."
>
> A young clerk from the owners' office asked whether this was strictly necessary.
>
> "It's never necessary," said the foreman. "That's why we do it."

## The Forging of the Sun

Only the outline of this myth is shared across the north. Veyr took a powerful material from beneath the world and forged the sun from it. He tried to contain it, to bind it to his purpose. The creation proved impossible to hold.

Veyr did not call it a failure. He cast it into the heavens, saying:

> *"Then let it burn where no roof can contain it."*

The lesson the Vards draw is that **a creation becoming something other than what its maker intended is not necessarily a failure**. It may be the best thing that could happen to it. Vardic engineers quote the line when an experiment surprises them, sometimes ruefully, sometimes with delight.

## Ragna's Last Voyage

Ragna sailed beyond the edge of the known world. She went so far that even the stars became unfamiliar. Her crew begged her to turn back. She kept going.

Much later, the ship came home. Ragna did not.

The traditional reading is that she is still travelling, somewhere beyond the known world. Since the Gates appeared, some Vards have begun to wonder whether the story was more literal than anyone assumed. Nobody knows, and the question is argued in every Vardic tavern in Endros. The story itself has never been more popular.

> **At a Gate threshold, Endros**
>
> The crew checked their gear one last time. The Vardic rigger said something under her breath, then a little louder, as if she had remembered she didn't care who heard.
>
> "Ragna, Far Shore. If you're out there, leave the way open for the rest of us."
>
> The Vernan surveyor beside her looked up from his notebook. "Do you really believe she went through something like this?"
>
> "I believe the ship came back," she said, and stepped through.

## The Nameless King

The darkest of the northern myths concerns a king who became obsessed with being remembered. He raised monuments to himself, demanded recognition, tried to erase rival stories and force his memory onto the world.

His punishment was not death. It was that **his name was taken out of remembrance**. His monuments are said to remain, but nobody knows whom they commemorate.

The lesson is plain to every Vard: *remembrance must be earned*. Demanding to be remembered is not the same as deserving it. Calling someone "a Nameless King" is a sharp insult in the Holds.

### The ruins theory

A small number of Vards, mostly enthusiasts rather than scholars, claim that the enormous **[[why-we-call-them-the-valeoran-ruins|Valeoran Ruins]]** around Endros could be connected to the Nameless King: vast monuments that nobody can attribute. Respectable scholars generally treat the idea as speculation driven by folklore. It is not established, and nothing has confirmed or ruled it out.

> **An argument in a dockside tavern in Endros**
>
> "Monuments nobody can name. Built to be seen from every horizon. Tell me who else that sounds like."
>
> "It sounds like every ruin before somebody reads the inscriptions."
>
> "And when nobody *can* read them?"
>
> "Then we haven't found the right page yet."
>
> "Or there was never a page. That was the punishment."
>
> The barkeep, who had heard this argument four times that week, refilled both cups and said nothing.

## Everyday Customs

The Old Gods are present in ordinary Vardic life far more often than in temples.

- **Named things.** Ships, engines, tools and weapons are often named, and a named object is treated with a certain respect. Destroying one carelessly is considered bad luck at best.
- **Oaths.** Serious promises are made before Haldor, aloud and in front of witnesses. Breaking one is not a private matter between two people. It damages your thread in the Weave, and everyone who heard it knows.
- **Remembrance.** Families keep ancestral halls, inscriptions and the deeds of the dead. Reciting what someone did is the simplest way of honouring them.
- **Expeditions.** Vardic Expeditioners speak Ragna's name before crossing into the unknown. Many put their maker's mark or their name on their gear, so that something carries their thread home even if they do not.

## The First Light in the Holds

The [[faith-of-the-first-light|Faith of the First Light]] is present in the Holds as a minority, imported tradition. It is most common in ports, trading towns and cosmopolitan settlements with strong foreign contact. Its exact form in the north varies, and it has no single Vardic communion of its own. The Old Gods remain the faith most Vards grow up with.

## The Old Gods and the Gates

The Gates have given the old stories new urgency. Ragna's Last Voyage is told in Endros as if it might be a field report. The Nameless King turns up in arguments about the ruins. And Veyr's words over the sun have become something close to a motto for Vardic Gate engineers: if a strange material will not do what you meant, perhaps it will do something better.

For the history of the Holds, including the people who made those engines, see [[the-vardic-holds|The Vardic Holds]].
